newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Left charges defence sell-out to U.S., NATO.
newsitem.headline: French Left charges defence sell-out to U.S., NATO.

text.p: The French Left accused the government on Wednesday of sacrificing national defence sovereignty to the United States and NATO in a joint strategy document signed with Germany.

Foreign Minister Herve de Charette dismissed the charge, saying the centre-right government was faithfully pursuing a Franco-German defence rapprochement begun by its predecessors, notably the late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand.

In an emergency parliamentary debate forced by the Left, Socialist floor leader Laurent Fabius said French policy "tends to bow more and more to American power at the risk of amputating the chances for a real European defence identity".

President Jacques Chirac and Chancellor Helmut Kohl approved the Joint Franco-German Security and Defence Concept on December 9 in Nuremberg. But it was given to French members of parliament only on Tuesday after a German text was leaked to the daily Le Monde last week.
Calling the two countries' security interests inseparable, it says their first commitment is to defend NATO and urges a dialogue on the role of nuclear deterrence in European defence.
Fabius accused the government of flouting parliamentary procedure by giving the document to NATO and European partners before sending it to French parliamentarians.
"What is happening is not the Europeanisation of NATO but, on the contrary, the NATO-isation of Europe," he said.

Like Socialist leader Lionel Jospin, Fabius criticised Chirac for agreeing to a fuller role in NATO, 30 years after General Charles de Gaulle pulled France out of its military wing, without winning any concessions from the United States.

Noting Chirac had called the Franco-German accord historic, Fabius said: "If 'historic' means that France, as the agreement suggests, must renounce part of its specialness, and that the European identity henceforth bends to the American empire, then we clearly do not agree to encourage that version of history."
However, he said the Socialists supported closer cooperation with Germany if it meant building a genuinely European defence.

Left-wing former defence minister Jean-Pierre Chevenement complained that France's independent nuclear deterrent was put on an equal footing in the text with a British nuclear arsenal that was entirely supplied by the United States.
Communist floor leader Alain Bocquet said the "secret accord, signed behind the people's backs" condemned France to play second fiddle to Germany in defence as in monetary affairs.
"This Nuremberg agreement is extremely dangerous for the sovereignty of France," he said.
Government speakers sought to play down any drama over the document, saying it mainly codified long-standing defence cooperation with France's closest European partner.
De Charette said there was absolutely nothing secret about the text, which was not a treaty but a declaration of intention.
"This text does not lend itself to polemics. If it changed French military doctrine in the slightest, you might have reason to worry. But it doesn't," he said.
Jacques Boyon, conservative Gaullist chairman of the National Assembly defence committee, said his first reaction to the document was "it's nothing to write home about".

"In its content, the Kohl-Chirac declaration is in fact only a reminder of the objectives pursued and the actions taken in the last few years by France and Germany in cooperation on military affairs and the defence industry," he said.
The brief, largely unemotional debate ended without a vote.
